title: Distributed Resource Theory of Entanglement and Magic
authors: Xiao Yuan, Wenhao Zhang, Qiming Ding, You Zhou
abstract: In distributed fault-tolerant quantum computing, entanglement and magic are essential resources for quantum communication and universal fault-tolerant computation, respectively. Although they are usually treated as distinct resource currencies, whether they admit a unified resource-theoretic description remains an open question. Here, we introduce the distributed resource theory of entanglement and magic (DREAM). In this framework, the free states are convex mixtures of product local stabilizer states, and the free operations are local stabilizer circuits assisted by classical communication (LSCC). We show that DREAM contains nontrivial resource states that are neither entanglement nor magic, so it is strictly richer than treating the two resources independently. Surprisingly, such resources can enable the teleportation of magic states between distant parties without consuming entanglement, revealing a counterintuitive form of resource teleportation mediated entirely by separable states. We further generalize this result to quantum networks and investigate general quantum-state teleportation under LSCC. We show that the shared resource under DREAM is closely related to the teleportation capability, quantified by the magic of the teleported state. Our work establish a systematic framework for studying distributed quantum resources and uncover intrinsic relations among distinct resources within a unified resource theory.
summary: This paper introduces the Distributed Resource Theory of Entanglement and Magic (DREAM) to unify the study of entanglement and magic in quantum computing. It proves that DREAM captures resources beyond what is captured by considering entanglement and magic separately. The work reveals counterintuitive resource behaviors, such as teleporting magic states using only separable resources.
main_problem: To develop a unified resource-theoretic description (DREAM) for entanglement and magic in distributed fault-tolerant quantum computing, determining if resources beyond these two are necessary.
main_result: DREAM is strictly richer than treating entanglement and magic independently, and a shared separable state can enable magic state teleportation without consuming entanglement.
method: The authors introduce the DREAM framework, defining free states based on local stabilizer circuits and analyzing resource flow using network flow analogies and robustness measures.
model_or_system: The study models quantum networks on a graph G=(V, E), involving local quantum systems, communication links, and resource states like magic states and general quantum states.
key_observables: Entanglement, Magic, DREAM Resourcefulness, Teleportation Capability, Maximal Free Weight ($w_{FAB}$)
important_parameters: The resource threshold $|t|$ for states $\Theta_{2k}(t)$ to be free under DREAM, and network capacities ($c_e, h_e$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the properties of local stabilizer circuits and the reduction of resource allocation problems to max-flow min-cut theorems.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the gate-level realization of the magic state teleportation protocol, and other figures relate resource flow to network cuts.
paper_structure: The paper systematically introduces DREAM, proves its strict resource richness, demonstrates counterintuitive resource teleportation protocols, and extends the analysis to general quantum networks using network flow theorems.
why_interesting: It establishes a powerful, unified mathematical framework for quantifying multiple, distinct quantum resources, which is highly relevant for designing fault-tolerant quantum computation protocols.
